recipe.history:
Asiago cheese takes its name from the Asiago plateau — the Altopiano di Asiago — in the Veneto region of northeastern Italy, a high alpine tableland at an elevation of roughly 1000 meters where dairy farming has been practiced since at least the tenth century. The earliest Asiago was made primarily from sheep's milk, but as cattle farming expanded on the plateau during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, cow's milk gradually became the dominant base. Asiago d'Allevo — the aged variety — is one of Italy's most ancient cheeses, matured for anywhere from two months (mezzano) to twelve or more months (vecchio and stravecchio), developing a pale amber paste and a flavor that transitions from mild and milky at two months to sharp, granular, and intensely savory — with notes of toasted nuts, caramel, and dried fruit — in its oldest form. The younger fresh version, Asiago Pressato, is a twentieth-century development, a softer, more supple cheese pressed into a milder form for markets that demanded a gentler product. Asiago received DOP (Denominazione di Origine Protetta) status from the European Union in 1996, formalizing the geographical boundaries of authentic production and protecting a cheese tradition that stretches back more than a thousand years in the shadow of the Dolomites.

Asiago arrived in the American market through the Italian immigrant communities of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, who carried not only the cheese but the cheesemaking knowledge to communities in Wisconsin, California, and the Northeast. American-made Asiago — produced primarily in Wisconsin dairy cooperatives — has been available in U.S. markets for over a century, and while it differs from authentic Italian Asiago DOP, it has developed its own distinct character: typically firmer, slightly sharper, and well-suited to grating and melting alike. The American deli and restaurant industry adopted Asiago as a sophisticated alternative to Parmesan for finishing pastas, topping focaccia, and, eventually, melting on burgers. The cheese's moderate sharpness and its excellent meltability — it flows smoothly without becoming greasy when heated — makes it a strong performer in burger applications, providing a funky, savory complexity that mild cheeses cannot deliver without overwhelming the beef.

I came to Asiago late, as far as burger cheeses go. For years I defaulted to cheddar, Gruyère, or American, convinced that Asiago was too sharp and too hard to behave well on a burger. The conversion happened at a small Italian-American restaurant in Providence, Rhode Island, where the chef served a burger topped with shaved aged Asiago and a drizzle of truffle honey — a combination I found alarming in description and extraordinary in execution. The shaved Asiago melted unevenly, some pieces becoming creamy and pooled while others remained in firm, slightly crispy curls against the hot patty surface. That textural variation — part melted, part barely warmed, all of it intensely savory — was something I had never experienced on a burger before, and it made me reconsider every assumption I had about how a burger cheese should behave. Since then I have used Asiago regularly, in both its fresh-pressed and aged forms, and I have never stopped being pleasantly surprised by how well it fits.

The medium-rare imperative gains a specific resonance on the Asiago burger because the cheese's assertive, nutty sharpness requires the beef to show up fully to the conversation. At 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C), the beef has a richness and a mineral depth — the flavors of well-raised, properly ground chuck — that can hold its own against aged Asiago without being overwhelmed. The interplay between the sharp, crystalline cheese and the yielding, juicy, pink-centered patty is one of contrasts: firm versus soft, sharp versus round, dry versus wet. These contrasts are the engine of a great burger. Cook the beef to well done and the contrasts flatten — there is no longer soft against firm, because both the cheese and the patty are dry and firm together. Medium rare is not preference. It is the condition under which this burger makes sense.
ingredients: 6 oz aged Asiago, thinly shaved with a vegetable peeler or mandoline
4 oz fresh Asiago Pressato, thinly sliced
1/2 cup oil-packed sun-dried tomatoes, drained and finely chopped
1 tbsp capers, rinsed and roughly chopped
Freshly cracked black pepper, to finish
High-quality extra-virgin olive oil, to drizzle
instructions: 1. Make the ciabatta-style buns: This is a wet, slack dough — do not be alarmed. Combine the yeast, warm water, and sugar and let bloom 5 minutes. Add the bread flour, salt, and olive oil. Mix with the dough hook on low 2 minutes, then medium for 6 to 8 minutes until the dough is elastic and comes away from the bowl sides in long strands, though it will remain wetter than a typical bread dough. Transfer to a well-oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled and full of bubbles.

2. Turn the risen dough onto a well-floured surface without punching it down — you want to preserve the gas bubbles. Using a bench scraper, cut into 4 rough rectangles approximately 4 by 5 inches each. Handle minimally. Transfer to a parchment-lined baking sheet dusted with semolina or flour, spacing well apart. Dust the tops generously with flour. Proof uncovered 30 to 45 minutes. Bake at 450°F (230°C) with steam (place a pan of hot water in the oven) for 20 to 22 minutes until hollow-sounding when tapped and the crust is golden and crisp. Cool completely before slicing horizontally.

3. Roast the garlic: Cut the top off the head of garlic to expose the cloves. Drizzle with olive oil, wrap in foil, and roast at 400°F (205°C) for 40 to 45 minutes until completely soft and golden. Cool, then squeeze the cloves into a bowl and mash to a smooth paste with a fork.
4. Make the roasted garlic aioli: Whisk together the roasted garlic paste, mayonnaise, lemon juice, salt, and pepper until smooth and fully combined. Refrigerate until assembly.

5. Make the sun-dried tomato relish: Stir together the chopped sun-dried tomatoes, fresh basil, capers, olive oil, red wine vinegar, red pepper flakes, and salt in a small bowl. Taste and adjust acid and salt. Set aside at room temperature.

6. Form the burger patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (8 oz / 227g each). Mix the salt, pepper, and dried oregano. Shape the beef gently into patties approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a dimple in the center. Season both sides with the seasoning blend immediately before cooking.

7. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip once. Immediately layer first the fresh Asiago Pressato slices, then a generous pile of the shaved aged Asiago, over each patty. Cover the pan and cook 2 to 3 more minutes until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) and the Asiago is melted — some pieces creamy and pooled, others slightly firm and lacy at the edges. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
8. Split the ciabatta buns and toast the cut sides on the hot skillet for 60 to 90 seconds until lightly golden and crisped.

9. Assemble: Spread the roasted garlic aioli on both bun halves. On the bottom bun, spoon the sun-dried tomato relish. Place the Asiago-crowned patty over the relish. Top with fresh basil leaves and arugula. Drizzle a thin thread of extra-virgin olive oil over the assembled toppings. Finish with freshly cracked black pepper. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
